translations.text: Listen! In days of old a wise sage, a prudent messenger, told me many rare wonders.

The man skilled in books unlocked his word-hoard, the teachings of the prophet, the ancient sayings of the messenger, so that afterwards I could truly recognise by that song God's own son, a welcome guest in human dwellings, and likewise tell apart the weaker one, cut off by his sins.

Anyone can easily think this through, as long as he does not let the wantonness of his heart, and drunkenness grown too powerful in the course of his days, spoil his mind in this passing time. For there are many speech-makers,

proud warriors in the wine-towns, who sit at the feast, recite true songs, and trade words with one another. They try to find out which place of battle will stay among the men inside the hall, when wine stirs up the heart in a man's breast.
Noise rises, uproar in the company, and voices ring out in all directions. In the same way minds are divided into separate parts, and men are not alike.
One man pushes forward with force in his pride, and an unrestrained mind swells within him. There are too many like that!

That envious man is completely filled with the devil's flying darts and treacherous snares. He shouts and belches, and boasts about himself far more than the better man does. He thinks everyone must find his conduct entirely beyond reproach.
Then there is another deceit in this, when he looks on the outcome of that treachery.
He twists and he dodges and thinks up many crafty tricks; he lets fly the spear of his mind and shoots in showers.

He does not know the guilt, the feud he has caused. Out of envy he hates a nobleman better than himself, and lets the arrows of malice break the city wall that the Lord ordered him to defend, that stronghold.

He sits proud at the feast and craftily lets his words, stirred up by wine, go out, forcing them out with violence. He is swollen with arrogance, burning with envy, full of pride, malice and narrow tricks.

Now you can recognize him. If you meet such a man living in the dwellings, know by these few first words that he is the child of the fiend, wrapped in flesh. He lives a wicked life, and his soul is hurrying to the abyss, cut off from God, the King of glory.
The prophet, a man ready with words, sang this and spoke this song: "He who in this cruel time lifts himself up through pride,
[?] exalts the proud man. He shall be brought low after his journey to death, bowed down, held fast in torments and surrounded by serpents.
Long ago in God's kingdom, pride arose among the angels, a strife known far and wide.

They raised up strife, a hard war-campaign; they [?] heaven. They despised their better when they plotted treachery and meant to rob the mighty King of glory of his princely throne, as was not right, and then to set up the joyful land of glory under their own rule.
Then the Father of creation opposed him in battle, and the fight became too fierce for him.

Then the one who lives humbly here on earth is unlike the other. He always keeps peace with each of his kinsmen among the people and loves his enemy, even though that enemy has often deliberately wronged him in this world.

That man may rise from here to the joy of glory, in the hope of the saints, to the land of the angels. It is not so for the other, who lives in vice, in arrogance and wicked deeds. Their rewards from the King of glory are not alike."
Know this from these words: if you meet a humble man, a thegn among the people, the Spirit, God's own son, welcome in the world, is always joined to him, if the prophet did not lie to me.
Therefore we must always think about the counsel of salvation, and keep in mind at every moment the best Ruler of victories. Amen.
